# Exercise: Hooke's Law Sensor data often come in multiple files. Possible reasons for this include measurements being taken * by different people, * at different locations, * at different times, * using different devices, or * for different measurement quantities. In the folder '01-daten/hooke', there are several txt files containing measurements of spring extension. In this chapter, you will apply what you have learned so far and answer the following questions: 1. Are there any invalid measurements? 2. What values can be determined for the spring constants? 3. Were the measurements taken with the same spring (or with springs of the same spring constant) if a confidence level of 90% or 95% is assumed? In section @sec-reading-files you will find guidance, and in section @sec-task-reading a sample solution for reading the files. Afterwards, you are expected to work on the tasks independently. Section @sec-solution-data-preparation provides a sample solution for data preprocessing. Section @sec-solution-springconstants contains the sample solution for determining the spring constants. *Note: Depending on the approach chosen, different results may arise (for example, when evaluating and handling extreme values / outliers).* ## Reading Files {#sec-reading-files} To read files, you can use the `glob` module (see [Module on Reading Structured Datasets](https://bausteine-der-datenanalyse.github.io/m-einlesen-strukturierter-datensaetze-en/output/book/)). First, you can pass the argument `pathname = *` to the function `glob.glob()`. The wildcard `*` stands for any sequence of characters (except path elements like `/` or `.`), allowing you to list all files stored in the specified folder. This way, you can determine the number of files and their extensions if they are not yet known. ::: {#bea4be61 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} folder_path = '01-daten/hooke' file_path_list = glob.glob(pathname='*', root_dir=folder_path, recursive=False) print(file_path_list) print(f"Number of files: {len(file_path_list)}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['team_fabi.txt', 'team_ma.txt', 'team_die_ahnungslosen.txt', 'team_kreativkoepfe.txt'] Number of files: 4 ``` ::: ::: Using the file paths, the files can be read into a list using a loop. Initially, only the first 3 rows of each file are read to get an impression of the file structure. ::: {#956e16a1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} for file_path in file_path_list: temp_storage = pd.read_csv(filepath_or_buffer = folder_path + '/' + file_path, nrows = 3) print(file_path, "\n", temp_storage, "\n", sep = '') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` team_fabi.txt 09:17:54\t110.31 cm\t0 0 09:17:57\t110.29 cm\t0 1 09:18:03\t110.74 cm\t0 2 09:18:06\t109.95 cm\t0 team_ma.txt 10:09:38\t109.26 cm\t0 0 10:09:41\t109.26 cm\t0 1 10:09:44\t109.28 cm\t0 2 10:09:47\t109.18 cm\t0 team_die_ahnungslosen.txt 11:03:23\t109.66 cm\t0 0 11:03:23\t109.62 cm\t0 1 11:03:23\t109.73 cm\t0 2 11:03:23\t109.55 cm\t0 team_kreativkoepfe.txt 10:33:02\t109.64 cm\t0 0 10:33:05\t109.62 cm\t0 1 10:33:08\t109.64 cm\t0 2 10:33:11\t109.62 cm\t0 ``` ::: ::: The files do not contain column headers and use the tab character `\t` as a delimiter. The first column contains a timestamp, the second the measured spring extension, and the third (presumably) the attached weight. ## Task: Reading Files {#sec-task-reading} Now read in the files. While doing so, check: - whether the data types are correctly interpreted, and - for missing values. You can: a) Read each file individually. b) Use the `glob` module to read the files automatically and store each in a separate object (*Note:* This approach is demonstrated in the [Module on Reading Structured Datasets](https://bausteine-der-datenanalyse.github.io/m-einlesen-strukturierter-datensaetze-en/output/book/)). c) Use the `glob` module to read the files automatically and merge them into a single file. These options require increasing levels of programming effort. The more separate files you want to analyze, the more automation is needed. Since sensor data analysis often involves numerous files, the model solution shows variant c). ::: {#tip-stepwise .callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Step-by-Step Approach Reading the files is likely to be the most time-consuming and error-prone step. Develop your solution step by step. Start with variant a). Once you have read the files, you can familiarize yourself with variant b) using the `glob` module. Building on that, variant c) allows you to automate the process for any number of files. ::: ::: {#tip-sample-files .callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model Solution: Reading Files The first attempt to read the files may fail with an error message. Therefore, the instructions are embedded in a try-except structure to catch the problematic file. (If multiple files cause errors, they would need to be stored in a list and processed later with a loop, if possible.) ::: {#a9d9e958 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} hooke = pd.DataFrame(columns = ['Time', 'Distance', 'Weight', 'Team']) # an empty DataFrame for path in file_path_list: try: temp_storage = pd.read_csv(filepath_or_buffer = folder_path + '/' + path, sep = '\t', names = ['Time', 'Distance', 'Weight']) # Add filename as a column temp_storage['Team'] = path[5:-4] # remove 'team_' and the file extension hooke = pd.concat([hooke, temp_storage], ignore_index = True) except Exception as error: print("Problematic file path: ", path, error, sep = "\n") problem_file_path = path print(hooke.info(), "\n") print("Successfully read:\n", hooke['Team'].unique(), sep = '') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Problematic file path: team_ma.txt Error tokenizing data. C error: Expected 3 fields in line 135, saw 4 RangeIndex: 359 entries, 0 to 358 Data columns (total 4 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 Time 355 non-null object 1 Distance 355 non-null object 2 Weight 355 non-null object 3 Team 359 non-null object dtypes: object(4) memory usage: 11.3+ KB None Successfully read: ['fabi' 'die_ahnungslosen' 'kreativkoepfe'] ``` ::: ::: According to the error message, line 135 contains 4 columns instead of 3. Therefore, the file causing the error is processed line by line, and each line with more than 3 entries is printed. For verification, the first 5 lines are also displayed. ::: {#81435047 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # create an empty DataFrame with 3 columns df = pd.DataFrame(data = [], columns = ['Time', 'Distance', 'Weight']) problem_file_object = open(file = folder_path + '/' + problem_file_path, mode = 'r') index = 0 for line in problem_file_object: try: buffer = line.split(sep = "\t") if len(buffer) > 3: print("Index =", index, ":", buffer) elif index <= 5: print(line) index += 1 except Exception as error: print(error) problem_file_object.close() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 10:09:38 109.26 cm 0 10:09:41 109.26 cm 0 10:09:44 109.28 cm 0 Index = 134 : ['10:29:27', '105.49 cm', '300', '\n'] ``` ::: ::: Every second line is empty. In line 134, a newline '\\n' is read. Therefore, the file is processed again using an adjusted loop. The extra newline '\\n' is removed from the relevant line. Empty lines are skipped. The correct lines are appended to the DataFrame 'hooke'. ::: {#86e81e15 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} problem_file_object = open(file = folder_path + '/' + problem_file_path, mode = 'r') for line in problem_file_object: try: buffer = line.split(sep = "\t") if len(buffer) > 3: buffer = buffer[:3] elif len(buffer) < 3: # skip empty lines continue # Append team name as 4th column buffer.append(problem_file_path[5:-4]) # remove 'team_' prefix and file extension hooke.loc[len(hooke)] = pd.Series(buffer).values except Exception as error: print(error) print(pd.Series(buffer).values) problem_file_object.close() print("Successfully read:\n", hooke['Team'].unique(), "\n", sep = '') print(hooke.info()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Successfully read: ['fabi' 'die_ahnungslosen' 'kreativkoepfe' 'ma'] Index: 537 entries, 0 to 536 Data columns (total 4 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 Time 533 non-null object 1 Distance 533 non-null object 2 Weight 533 non-null object 3 Team 537 non-null object dtypes: object(4) memory usage: 21.0+ KB None ``` ::: ::: Next, we look at the rows that contain null values ... ::: {#29132284 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(hooke.loc[hooke.apply(pd.isna).any(axis=1), :]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Time Distance Weight Team 207 NaN NaN NaN die_ahnungslosen 247 NaN NaN NaN kreativkoepfe 267 NaN NaN NaN kreativkoepfe 272 NaN NaN NaN kreativkoepfe ``` ::: ::: ... and removed. ::: {#ef6dbd9e .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} hooke.drop(np.where(hooke.apply(pd.isna).any(axis=1))[0], inplace=True) ``` ::: Next, the data types are checked. - The time can remain as a string, since it is not needed for the analysis. - The measured distance is noted with ' cm' – this string will be removed. Afterwards, the column should be recognized as numeric. - The weight should contain numeric values, but is read in as an object type and needs further investigation. - The Team column could be assigned the [Pandas category datatype](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/categorical.html), but this is not necessary. Remove the string ' cm'. ::: {#77872415 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} hooke.replace(' cm', '', regex = True, inplace = True) ``` ::: You can check if all elements of a column are numeric using the Pandas method `pd.Series.str.isnumeric()`. A look at the data shows the cause. ::: {#2f42b9bf .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(hooke['Weight'].str.isnumeric().sum()) print(hooke['Weight'].head()) print(hooke['Weight'].tail()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 0 0 1 0 2 0 3 0 4 0 Name: Weight, dtype: object 532 850\n 533 850\n 534 850\n 535 850\n 536 850\n Name: Weight, dtype: object ``` ::: ::: The line breaks are also removed. ::: {#ea499f35 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} hooke.replace('\n', '', regex=True, inplace=True) print(hooke['Weight'].str.isnumeric().sum()) print(hooke['Weight'].tail()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 178 532 850 533 850 534 850 535 850 536 850 Name: Weight, dtype: object ``` ::: ::: ::: {#96ddaf69 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(hooke.info(), "\n") # explicit assignment hooke['Distance'] = hooke['Distance'].astype('float') hooke['Weight'] = hooke['Weight'].astype('float') print(hooke.info()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Index: 533 entries, 0 to 536 Data columns (total 4 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 Time 533 non-null object 1 Distance 533 non-null object 2 Weight 533 non-null object 3 Team 533 non-null object dtypes: object(4) memory usage: 20.8+ KB None Index: 533 entries, 0 to 536 Data columns (total 4 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 Time 533 non-null object 1 Distance 533 non-null float64 2 Weight 533 non-null float64 3 Team 533 non-null object dtypes: float64(2), object(2) memory usage: 20.8+ KB None ``` ::: ::: ::: The result might look like this: ::: {#058b9c7c .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} hooke.groupby(by = ['Team', 'Weight'], sort = False)['Distance'].describe() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Sample Solution: Data Preparation {#sec-solution-data-preparation} In the next step, the data will be checked and, if necessary, cleaned. This includes the following steps: - checking for outliers (using studentized z-scores and visually) and cleaning if necessary, - normalizing the distance measurement to the zero point and converting the units used to SI units, and - graphical representation. ::: {#wrn-globgroupby .callout-warning appearance="simple"} ## glob, pd.groupby, and SciPy The execution of the following code may vary locally, depending on the order in which files are read using the glob module. In the following, index positions in a groupby object are determined where a condition is true. These index positions are then used to access the original DataFrame. Pandas sorts the groups in a groupby object alphabetically by default (`sort=True`). If the files read with glob are not in alphabetical order, incorrect index positions may be used to access the DataFrame. This can be avoided either by sorting the DataFrame according to the groupby criteria or, as shown here, by using the argument `pd.groupby(by=condition, sort=False)`. The latter approach is more flexible. Also, `scipy.stats.zscore()` may return either a `pd.Series` or a `np.array` depending on the version. Accordingly, methods from Pandas or NumPy should be used. ::: 1. **Are there invalid measurements?** ### Checking for Outliers Outliers can be checked (among other methods) using studentized z-scores and visually. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Determining Outliers 1. Determine the number of outliers and display their positions. ::: {#fedc874c .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Find z-scores greater than or equal to abs(3) ## Solution for SciPy 1.14.1 (returns pd.Series) ## z_values_ge3_sum = hooke.groupby(by=['Team', 'Weight'])['Distance'].apply(lambda x: scipy.stats.zscore(x, ddof=1)).abs().ge(3).sum() ## Solution for SciPy 1.15 and later (returns np.array) z_values_ge3_sum = hooke.groupby(by=['Team', 'Weight'], sort=False)['Distance'].apply(scipy.stats.zscore, ddof=1).apply(np.abs).apply(lambda x: np.greater_equal(x, 3)).apply(sum).sum() print("Number of studentized z-scores with absolute value ≥ 3:", z_values_ge3_sum, "\n") # Find z-scores greater than or equal to abs(2.5) ## Solution for SciPy 1.14.1 (returns pd.Series) ## z_values_ge25_sum = hooke.groupby(by=['Team', 'Weight'])['Distance'].apply(lambda x: scipy.stats.zscore(x, ddof=1)).abs().ge(2.5).sum() ## Solution for SciPy 1.15 and later (returns np.array) z_values_ge25_sum = hooke.groupby(by=['Team', 'Weight'], sort=False)['Distance'].apply(scipy.stats.zscore, ddof=1).apply(np.abs).apply(lambda x: np.greater_equal(x, 2.5)).apply(sum).sum() print("Number of studentized z-scores with absolute value ≥ 2.5:", z_values_ge25_sum) # Display rows with z-scores greater than abs(2.5) ## Solution for SciPy 1.14.1 (returns pd.Series) ## bool_index = hooke.groupby(by=['Team', 'Weight'])['Distance'].apply(lambda x: scipy.stats.zscore(x, ddof=1)).abs().ge(2.5).values ## Solution for SciPy 1.15 and later (returns np.array) ### Step 1: Capture boolean values bool_index = hooke.groupby(by=['Team', 'Weight'], sort=False)['Distance'].apply(scipy.stats.zscore, ddof=1).apply(np.abs).apply(lambda x: np.greater_equal(x, 2.5)).values ### Step 2: Flatten to a 1D array bool_index = np.hstack(bool_index) print("\nOutliers are located at these index positions:", np.nonzero(bool_index)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of studentized z-scores with absolute value ≥ 3: 0 Number of studentized z-scores with absolute value ≥ 2.5: 4 Outliers are located at these index positions: (array([ 44, 186, 201, 206]),) ``` ::: ::: 2.
